verses.zh: 主耶和华又指示我一件事：我看见一筐夏天的果子。
verses.en: The Sovereign Lord showed me this: I saw[NOTE:1] a basket of summer fruit.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “behold” or “look.”
The basket of summer fruit (also in the following verse) probably refers to figs from the summer crop, which ripens in August-September. See O. Borowski, Agriculture in Iron Age Israel, 115.

verses.zh: 他说：「阿摩司啊，你看见甚么？」我说：「看见一筐夏天的果子。」耶和华说：「我民以色列的结局到了，我必不再宽恕他们。」
verses.en: He said, “What do you see, Amos?” I replied, “A basket of summer fruit.” Then the Lord said to me, “The end[NOTE:1] has come for my people Israel! I will no longer overlook their sins.[NOTE:2]
notes: There is a sound play here. The Hebrew word קֵץ (qets, “end”) sounds like קָיִץ (qayits, “summer fruit”). Possibly they were pronounced alike in the Northern dialect of Hebrew. This is a case where the vision is not the prophecy, but simply the occasion for a prophecy. The basket of summer fruit is only relevant as a means to get Amos to say qayits (קָיִץ) as an occasion for the Lord to say qets (קֵץ) and make the prophecy. Cf. Jer 1:11-14; Amos 7:7-8.
Heb “I will no longer pass over him.”

verses.zh: 主耶和华说：「那日，殿中的诗歌变为哀号；必有许多尸首在各处抛弃，无人作声。」
verses.en: The women singing in the temple[NOTE:1] will wail in that day.” The Sovereign Lord is speaking. “There will be many corpses littered everywhere![NOTE:2] Be quiet!”
notes: Or “palace” (NASB, NCV, TEV).

Heb “Many corpses in every place he will throw out.” The subject of the verb is probably impersonal, though many emend the active (Hiphil) form to a passive (Hophal): “Many corpses in every place will be thrown out.”

verses.zh: 你们这些要吞吃穷乏人、使困苦人衰败的，当听我的话！
verses.en: Listen to this, you who trample[NOTE:1] the needyand do away with[NOTE:2] the destitute in the land.
notes: See the note on the word “trample” in 2:7.
Or “put an end to”; or “exterminate.”

verses.zh: 你们说：月朔几时过去，我们好卖粮；安息日几时过去，我们好摆开麦子；卖出用小升斗，收银用大戥子，用诡诈的天平欺哄人，
verses.en: You say, “When will the new moon festival[NOTE:1] be over,[NOTE:2] so we can sell grain? When will the Sabbath end,[NOTE:3] so we can open up the grain bins?[NOTE:4] We’re eager[NOTE:5] to sell less for a higher price,[NOTE:6] and to cheat the buyer with rigged scales![NOTE:7]
notes: Apparently work was prohibited during the new moon festival, just as it was on the Sabbath.
Heb “pass by.”
The verb, though omitted in the Hebrew text, is supplied in the translation from the parallel line.
Heb “sell grain.” Here “grain” could stand by metonymy for the bins where it was stored.
Here and in v. 6 the words “we’re eager” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

Heb “to make small the ephah and to make great the shekel.” The “ephah” was a unit of dry measure used to determine the quantity purchased, while the “shekel” was a standard weight used to determine the purchase price. By using a smaller than standard ephah and a heavier than standard shekel, these merchants were able to increase their profit (“sell less for a higher price”) by cheating the buyer.

Rigged scales may refer to bending the crossbar or shifting the center point of the scales to make the amount weighed appear heavier than it actually was, thus cheating the buyer.tn Heb “and to cheat with deceptive scales”; cf. NASB, NIV “dishonest scales,” NRSV “false balances.”

verses.zh: 好用银子买贫寒人，用一双鞋换穷乏人，将坏了的麦子卖给人。
verses.en: We’re eager to trade silver for the poor,[NOTE:1] a pair of sandals[NOTE:2] for the needy.We want to mix in some chaff with the grain!”[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “to buy the poor for silver.”sn The expression trade silver for the poor refers to the slave trade.
See the note on the word “sandals” in 2:6.
Heb “The chaff of the grain we will sell.”

verses.zh: 耶和华指着雅各的荣耀起誓说：他们的一切行为，我必永远不忘。
verses.en: The Lord confirms this oath[NOTE:1] by the arrogance of Jacob:[NOTE:2] “I swear[NOTE:3] I will never forget all you have done![NOTE:4]
notes: Or “swears.”

In an oath one appeals to something permanent to emphasize one’s commitment to the promise. Here the Lord sarcastically swears by the arrogance of Jacob, which he earlier had condemned (6:8), something just as enduring as the Lord’s own life (see 6:8) or unchanging character (see 4:2). Other suggestions include that the Lord is swearing by the land, his most valuable possession (cf. Isa 4:2; Ps 47:4 [47:5 HT]); that this is a divine epithet analogous to “the Glory of Israel” (1 Sam 15:29); or that an ellipsis should be understood here, in which case the meaning is the same as that of 6:8 (“The Lord has sworn [by himself] against the arrogance of Jacob”).
The words “I swear” are not in the Hebrew text but have been supplied in the translation because a self-imprecation is assumed in oaths of this type.
Or “I will never forget all your deeds.”

verses.zh: 地岂不因这事震动？其上的居民不也悲哀吗？地必全然像尼罗河涨起，如同埃及河涌上落下。
verses.en: Because of this the earth[NOTE:1] will quake,[NOTE:2] and all who live in it will mourn.The whole earth[NOTE:3] will rise like the Nile River;[NOTE:4] it will surge upward[NOTE:5] and then grow calm,[NOTE:6] like the Nile in Egypt.[NOTE:7]
notes: Or “land” (also later in this verse).
It is not clear whether the speaker in this verse is the Lord or the prophet.
Heb “all of it.”

The movement of the quaking earth is here compared to the annual flooding and receding of the Nile River.tc The MT reads “like the light” (כָאֹר, khaʾor; note this term also appears in v. 9), which is commonly understood to be an error for “like the Nile” (כִּיאוֹר, kiʾor). See the parallel line and Amos 9:5. The word “River” is supplied in the translation for clarity. If this emendation is correct, in the Hebrew of Amos “Nile” is actually spelled three slightly different ways.
Or “churn.”
Or “sink back down.” The translation assumes the verb שָׁקַע (shaqaʿ), following the Qere.

The entire verse is phrased in a series of rhetorical questions that anticipate the answer, “Of course!” (For example, the first line reads, “Because of this will the earth not quake?”). The rhetorical questions entrap the listener in the logic of the judgment of God (cf. 3:3-6; 9:7). The rhetorical questions have been converted to affirmative statements in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 主耶和华说：到那日，我必使日头在午间落下，使地在白昼黑暗。
verses.en: In that day,” says the Sovereign Lord, “I will make the sun set at noonand make the earth dark in the middle of the day.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “in a day of light.”

verses.zh: 我必使你们的节期变为悲哀，歌曲变为哀歌。众人腰束麻布，头上光秃，使这场悲哀如丧独生子，至终如痛苦的日子一样。
verses.en: I will turn your festivals into funerals[NOTE:1] and all your songs into funeral dirges.I will make everyone wear funeral clothes[NOTE:2] and cause every head to be shaved bald.[NOTE:3] I will make you mourn as if you had lost your only son;[NOTE:4] when it ends it will indeed have been a bitter day.[NOTE:5]
notes: Heb “mourning.”
Heb “I will place sackcloth on all waists.”sn Mourners wore sackcloth (funeral clothes) as an outward expression of grief.

Shaving the head or tearing out one’s hair was a ritual act of mourning. See Lev 21:5; Deut 14:1; Isa 3:24; 15:2; Jer 47:5; 48:37; Ezek 7:18; 27:31; Mic 1:16.tn Heb “and make every head bald.” This could be understood in a variety of ways, while the ritual act of mourning typically involved shaving the head (although occasionally the hair could be torn out as a sign of mourning).
Heb “I will make it like the mourning for an only son.”
Heb “and its end will be like a bitter day.” The Hebrew preposition כְּ (kaf) sometimes carries the force of “in every respect,” indicating identity rather than mere comparison.

verses.zh: 主耶和华说：日子将到，我必命饥荒降在地上。人饥饿非因无饼，干渴非因无水，乃因不听耶和华的话。
verses.en: Be certain of this,[NOTE:1] the time is[NOTE:2] coming,” says the Sovereign Lord, “when I will send a famine through the land—not a shortage of food or waterbut an end to divine revelation.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “behold” or “look.”
Heb “the days are.”
Heb “not a hunger for food or a thirst for water, but for hearing the words of the Lord.”

verses.zh: 他们必飘流，从这海到那海，从北边到东边，往来奔跑，寻求耶和华的话，却寻不着。
verses.en: People[NOTE:1] will stagger from sea to sea,[NOTE:2] and from the north around to the east. They will wander about looking for a message from the Lord, but they will not find any.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “they”; the referent (people) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
That is, from the Mediterranean Sea in the west to the Dead Sea in the east—namely, across the whole land.
It is not clear whether the speaker in this verse is the Lord or the prophet.

verses.zh: 当那日，美貌的处女和少年的男子必因干渴发昏。
verses.en: In that day your[NOTE:1] beautiful young women[NOTE:2] and your[NOTE:3] young men will faint from thirst.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “the.”
Or “virgins.”
Heb “the.”
It is not clear whether the speaker in this verse is the Lord or the prophet.

verses.zh: 那指着撒马利亚牛犊（原文是罪）起誓的说：但哪，我们指着你那里的活神起誓；又说：我们指着别是巴的神道（神：原文是活）起誓。这些人都必仆倒，永不再起来。
verses.en: These are the ones who now take oaths[NOTE:1] in the name of the sinful idol goddess[NOTE:2] of Samaria. They vow,[NOTE:3] ‘As surely as your god[NOTE:4] lives, O Dan,’ or, ‘As surely as your beloved one[NOTE:5] lives, O Beer Sheba!’ But they will fall down and not get up again.”
notes: Heb “those who swear.”

Heb “the sin [or “guilt”] of Samaria.” This could be a derogatory reference to an idol-goddess popular in the northern kingdom, perhaps Asherah (cf. 2 Chr 24:18, where this worship is labeled “their guilt”), or to the golden calf at the national sanctuary in Bethel (Hos 8:6; 10:8). Some English versions (e.g., NEB, NRSV, CEV) repoint the word and read “Ashimah,” the name of a goddess worshiped in Hamath in Syria (see 2 Kgs 17:30).
Heb “say.”

Your god is not identified. It may refer to another patron deity who was not the God of Israel, a local manifestation of the Lord that was worshiped by the people there, or, more specifically, the golden calf image erected in Dan by Jeroboam I (see 1 Kgs 12:28-30).

The MT reads, “As surely as the way [to] Beer Sheba lives,” or “As surely as the way lives, O Beer Sheba.” Perhaps the term דֶּרֶךְ (derekh, “the way”) refers to the pilgrimage route to Beersheba (see S. M. Paul, Amos [Hermeneia], 272), or it may be a title for a god. The notion of pilgrimage appears elsewhere in the book (cf. 4:4-5; 5:4-5; 8:12). The translation above assumes an emendation to דֹּדְךָ (dodekha, “your beloved” or “relative”; the term also is used in 6:10) and understands this as referring either to the Lord (since other kinship terms are used of him, such as “Father”) or to another deity that was particularly popular in Beer Sheba. Besides the commentaries, see S. M. Olyan, “The Oaths of Amos 8:14” Priesthood and Cult in Ancient Israel, 121-49.
